title: Growing old: how a body changes from baby to elder

summary.text: A grandmother holds her phone far from her face to read it, while a child reads it close up. Every person goes through the same stages: baby, child, teenager, adult and older adult. As the years pass, hair turns grey, skin springs back more slowly, and the lens in the eye gets stiffer. Your body makes millions of new cells every second, but some parts, like the middle of the eye lens, are never replaced. Scientists still argue about why bodies age at all.
summary.art: One long line of hands laid side by side on a wooden table: a tiny baby's hand, a child's hand, a teenager's, a parent's and a wrinkled grandparent's hand with a silver ring.

intro.hook: Look at the back of your hand. Now look at the back of the hand of the oldest person in your home. What is different? What is the same?
intro.text: Every grandparent you know was once a baby. They had no teeth. They could not walk. Their head was huge compared to their body. One day you will be as old as them. Your hair may turn white, and your skin may fold into soft lines. Why does a body change like this? And how much of you is new, and how much is as old as you are?
intro.art: A grandmother and a child sitting side by side on a charpai, both holding the back of their hands up to compare, sunlight on both.

outcomes: I can name the stages of a human life in order: baby, child, teenager, adult and older adult.
I can describe how a body changes at each stage, using examples like teeth, height, hair, skin and eyes.
I can run a fair test that compares people of different ages, and show the results in a table and a bar chart.
I can explain that the body is always making new cells, but some cells stay with us all our lives.
I can say what gets harder and what can get better as people grow old, and how we can help elders.
I can say what scientists agree about ageing, and what they still argue about.
I can talk gently about the end of a life as part of every life cycle.
I can explain big ideas about ageing: tiny caps on our genes, a grandmother idea, and animals that barely seem to age.

terms.meaning: All the stages a living thing goes through, from the start of its life to the end.
terms.example: A mango tree starts as a seed, grows, makes mangoes with new seeds, grows old and one day dies.
terms.art: A circle of arrows: seed, sapling, mango tree with fruit, old tree, fallen seeds.

terms.meaning: One part of a life cycle, when the body is a certain way.
terms.example: Being a baby is one life stage. Being a grandparent is often another.
terms.art: Five steps going up: baby, child, teenager, adult, older adult.

terms.meaning: A baby in its first year of life.
terms.example: Your baby cousin who cannot walk yet is an infant.
terms.art: A baby lying on a cotton mat, kicking its legs.

terms.meaning: A person aged about 13 to 19. Their body grows fast and changes into a grown-up shape.
terms.example: An older cousin whose voice is getting deeper is a teenager.
terms.art: A tall teenager next to a pencil mark on a door frame much higher than last year's mark.

terms.meaning: A person whose body has finished growing taller. In India, a person is called an adult in law from age 18.
terms.example: Your parents and teachers are adults.
terms.art: Two adults carrying shopping bags from a sabzi market.

terms.meaning: A person in the later part of life, often over 60. Many elders are grandparents.
terms.example: A grandmother who has lived 70 years is an older adult.
terms.art: An elderly man with white hair reading a newspaper held far from his face.

terms.meaning: The slow changes a body goes through as the years pass.
terms.example: Grey hair and reading glasses are signs of ageing.
terms.art: The same face drawn at 10, 40 and 75 years old.

terms.meaning: The tiny living building block that bodies are made of. Most cells are too small to see without a microscope.
terms.example: Your skin, blood and bones are all made of cells.
terms.art: A zoomed-in circle on a hand showing tiny round skin cells like bricks.

terms.meaning: A strong, stretchy material in skin that makes it springy. The body makes less of it as we get older.
terms.example: A young child's skin springs back fast when pinched, because it has lots of collagen.
terms.art: Skin drawn like a mattress, with springy threads inside.

terms.meaning: A material that gives something its colour. The pigment in hair and skin is called melanin.
terms.example: Black hair has lots of dark pigment. White hair has almost none.
terms.art: Three strands of hair: black, grey and white, with dots of colour inside the black one.

terms.meaning: The clear, bendy part inside your eye. It changes shape so that things look sharp.
terms.example: When you read a book up close, your lens gets fatter to make the words sharp.
terms.art: A drawing of an eye with a clear bean-shaped lens inside it.

terms.meaning: The closest distance at which you can still see something sharply.
terms.example: A child can read a page 10 cm from the nose. Many grandparents need it 50 cm away.
terms.art: A child holding a book close and a grandfather holding one at arm's length.

terms.meaning: How long a living thing lives, from birth to death.
terms.example: The longest checked human lifespan is 122 years.
terms.art: A long ribbon marked with years, with a tiny baby at one end.

terms.meaning: How many years, on average, people born in a certain place and time are expected to live.
terms.example: In India today, life expectancy is about 70 years.
terms.art: Two bars, a short one for India in 1951 and a long one for India today.

terms.meaning: The body making new cells to replace old or worn-out ones.
terms.example: The outer layer of your skin is replaced about every month.
terms.art: Tiny old skin flakes falling off as new skin cells push up from below.

terms.meaning: When a living thing's body stops working for good. It is the last part of every life cycle.
terms.example: Old leaves fall from a tree and become soil. A very old pet may die peacefully.
terms.art: A dry leaf resting on soil, with a small green sprout beside it.

explanations.definition: Every human life goes through the same stages in the same order: baby, child, teenager, adult and older adult.
explanations.description: Nobody skips a stage. Everybody you know is in one of them right now. The stages do not have sharp edges. Nobody wakes up one morning and is suddenly a teenager. Bodies change slowly, a little every day. Each stage also has its own jobs. Babies learn to walk and talk. Children learn and play. Adults often work and care for others. Elders often teach, remember and help raise the young.
examples: Your grandmother was a baby, then a girl, then a young woman, then a mother, and now a grandmother.
A newborn baby needs others for everything. An 8-year-old can dress and feed themselves.
A mango tree and a dog also have life stages, but they move through them at different speeds.
explanations.art: A winding path through a village with the same person shown at five stages along it, from crawling baby to grandmother with a walking stick.
explanations.context: This card gives the big picture of the whole unit: the stages of a human life.

explanations.definition: A baby's body is not a small adult body. It has different proportions, softer bones and it grows faster than at any other time of life.
explanations.description: A newborn is about 50 centimetres long. By its first birthday it is about 75 centimetres. That is the fastest growing a person ever does. A baby's head is about one quarter of its whole length. In an adult, the head is only about one eighth. A baby's skull has soft spots, where the bones have not joined yet. This lets the skull grow with the brain. A baby is born with about 300 bones and soft parts that will become bone. Many of them join together as the child grows. An adult has 206 bones.
examples: A baby's arms are so short it cannot touch the top of its own head.
Baby teeth are already hiding inside a baby's gums at birth.
A newborn's soft spot on top of the head closes by about age two.
explanations.art: A baby and an adult drawn side by side, scaled to the same height, showing the baby's much bigger head.
explanations.context: This card explains how a baby's body differs from a grown-up's body.

explanations.concept: Childhood and the teenage growth spurt
explanations.definition: In childhood the body grows steadily, about 5 to 6 centimetres a year. In the teenage years it grows fast again, then stops growing taller.
explanations.description: Between about age 6 and 12, milk teeth fall out and adult teeth grow in. Bones get longer at their ends, in places called growth plates. In the teenage years there is a growth spurt, a time of very fast growing. Bodies also slowly change into a grown-up shape. Then the growth plates close and turn to solid bone. After that, a person does not grow taller any more. This usually happens by the late teens or early twenties.
examples: An older cousin may grow 8 or 10 centimetres in one year as a teenager.
Losing a milk tooth at 6 or 7 is a sign the body is moving on to the next stage.
Your feet often grow fast before the rest of you does, so shoes stop fitting first.
explanations.art: A door frame with pencil marks and ages written beside them, the marks close together low down and then a big jump higher up.
explanations.context: This card explains how bodies grow during childhood and the teenage years.

explanations.definition: Adults have stopped growing taller. Their bodies are usually at their strongest in their twenties and thirties, and then begin to change slowly.
explanations.description: In the twenties and thirties, muscles, bones, heart and lungs are usually at their strongest. Bones are at their thickest at about age 30. From around age 40, small changes begin. Many people notice they need to hold small print further away. A few grey hairs may appear. Muscles slowly shrink if they are not used. These changes are slow and different for every person. Exercise, good food, sleep and friends make a big difference at every age.
examples: Many top runners and footballers are in their twenties.
Your parent may have started wearing reading glasses at about 40 or 45.
A farmer of 50 who works in the fields every day can be stronger than an office worker of 30 who sits all day.
explanations.art: An adult woman jogging in a park in the morning, with an older man doing yoga on the grass behind her.
explanations.context: This card explains what happens to bodies in the grown-up years, between the teenage years and old age.

explanations.definition: Hair turns grey and white when the cells at the root of each hair stop making colour, called pigment.
explanations.description: Each hair grows from a tiny pocket in the skin. In that pocket are pigment cells. They put colour into the hair as it grows. As we get older, these cells slowly run out. The new hair grows without colour, so it is white. A head with some dark hairs and some white hairs looks grey from far away. A hair that has already grown cannot change colour. Only new hair grows in white. Your genes decide a lot about when this starts. Some people go grey at 30, others at 70.
examples: A grandparent's 'grey' hair is really a mix of white and dark hairs.
Eyebrows and beards can turn grey too, because they are also hair.
Dogs often get white hairs around the nose when they are old.
explanations.art: A zoomed-in drawing of one hair root under the skin, with small pigment cells colouring a dark hair, beside an empty root growing a white hair.
explanations.context: This card explains why many older people have grey or white hair.

explanations.definition: Skin wrinkles because, over many years, it gets thinner, drier and less springy.
explanations.description: Inside your skin are stretchy threads called collagen and elastin. They work like the springs in a mattress. They make skin bounce back when you pinch it. Most elastin is made while you are young, and the body makes very little later. So many of the springy threads in an elder's skin are as old as the elder. As people get older, the body also makes less collagen. Skin makes less oil, so it gets drier. Strong sunlight over many years breaks the threads faster. So older skin folds and springs back slowly. The lines often form where we smile and frown the most.
examples: Skin on the back of a young child's hand snaps back fast when pinched. An elder's skin flattens slowly.
Farmers who work in strong sun often get wrinkles earlier.
The lines at the corners of a grandmother's eyes show where she has laughed most.
explanations.art: Two drawings of skin cut open: young skin with tight, springy coils, and older skin with thinner, looser coils and soft folds on top.
explanations.context: This card explains why skin gets wrinkles as people grow old.

explanations.concept: Why older eyes hold books far away
explanations.definition: As people get older, the lens inside the eye gets stiffer. A stiff lens cannot focus on things that are close, so small print looks blurry.
explanations.description: To see something close, a tiny muscle lets the lens in your eye get fatter and rounder. Then the close thing looks sharp. A child's lens is soft, like jelly, and changes shape easily. The lens never throws away old cells. All through life it adds new layers around the old ones, so it gets thicker and stiffer every year. By about age 45, most people cannot see small print sharply at a normal reading distance. So they hold the newspaper further away. Reading glasses do the extra focusing for them. Far-away things usually still look sharp. Doctors call this change presbyopia, from a Greek word for an old man.
examples: A child can read a book held 10 centimetres from the nose.
A grandfather may hold his phone at arm's length to read a message.
Reading glasses are often sold at chemist shops in steps like +1, +2 and +3.
explanations.art: Two eyes drawn from the side: a child's eye with a round, soft lens, and an older eye with a flatter, stiffer lens and blurred letters in front.
explanations.context: This card explains why many older people need reading glasses or hold small print far away.

explanations.definition: As years pass, ears hear high sounds less well, bones get thinner, muscles get smaller and joints get stiffer. Using the body slows these changes down.
explanations.description: Deep inside the ear are tiny hair cells that pick up sounds. The ones for very high sounds wear out first. So many older people hear high voices and whistles less well. Bones slowly lose some of their hard minerals, so they break more easily in a fall. Muscles get smaller if they are not used. Joints, like knees, can get stiff and sore. But here is the good news. Muscles can grow stronger at any age. In 1990, scientists in Boston gave strength exercises to people aged about 90. In eight weeks, their muscles got much stronger.
examples: A grandparent may ask you to repeat what you said, especially in a noisy room.
Older people often walk carefully on wet floors, because a fall can break a bone.
Many elders in Indian parks do yoga and walk every morning to keep strong.
explanations.art: An elderly woman lifting a small water bottle like a weight while her grandson counts, both smiling.
explanations.context: This card explains how ears, bones, muscles and joints change in old age, and what helps.

explanations.concept: What keeps growing as we get older
explanations.description: Not everything gets weaker with age. Some things keep growing. Scientists have tested thousands of people of all ages on puzzles and words. Quick puzzles were done fastest by people in their late teens and twenties. But the number of words people knew kept rising until their sixties and seventies. Elders also know a lot from experience, like how to calm a crying baby or what to do in a flood. Some studies find that many older people feel calmer and happier than middle-aged people. Other studies disagree, so this part is still an idea.
examples: Your grandparent may know the names of plants, songs and festivals that nobody else in the family remembers.
In 2018, Karthyayani Amma of Kerala took a literacy exam at age 96 and scored 98 out of 100.
An old carpenter can often tell good wood by touch, faster than any young worker.

perspectives.explanation: Knowledge, words and some kinds of wisdom keep growing well into old age, even while speed slows down.
How happy and calm people feel in old age differs hugely by country, health, money and friends. We cannot say all elders feel happier.

explanations.art: An elderly woman at a kitchen table teaching a child a song from a notebook full of handwritten recipes and songs.
explanations.context: This card is about the things that can keep growing as people get older, not only the things that get harder.

explanations.concept: Your body is always rebuilding itself
explanations.definition: Your body is made of about 37 trillion cells. Every second, it makes millions of new ones to replace old ones.
explanations.description: Scientists estimate your body makes about 4 million new cells every second. Most are blood cells. A red blood cell lasts about four months. The outer layer of your skin is replaced about every month. The lining of your stomach and gut is replaced every few days. Your whole skeleton is slowly rebuilt over about ten years. But not every cell is replaced. Most cells in the thinking part of your brain stay with you all your life. The cells in the middle of your eye lens were made before you were born. So some parts of you are a few days old, and some are older than you are.
examples: The dust in your home is partly old skin flakes, from everyone who lives there.
A cut on your knee heals because new skin cells grow to fill the gap.
Scientists found how old brain cells are by measuring a kind of carbon left in the air by bomb tests in the 1950s and 1960s.
explanations.art: A child's body outline filled with tiny dots, some glowing new and some staying old, with labels: skin new each month, blood new every four months, eye lens as old as you.
explanations.context: This card explains that your body is always making new cells, even though you feel like the same person.

explanations.concept: Why do bodies age at all?
explanations.description: Scientists know a lot about how bodies age. They still argue about why. Here are the main ideas. Many scientists think more than one of them is true at once.
examples: Most of your cells can only split to make new cells a certain number of times. In 1961, Leonard Hayflick and Paul Moorhead found human cells in a dish stopped after about 40 to 60 splits.
Elizabeth Blackburn and Carol Greider found telomerase, a substance that rebuilds the caps on the ends of genes. They shared a Nobel Prize in 2009 with Jack Szostak.
A mouse lives about 2 years. A human can live 80 or more. Their cells are very alike, so the timetable must be set partly by genes.

perspectives.explanation: Every day, tiny bits of damage happen inside cells. The body repairs most of it. Over many years, a little damage builds up faster than it is fixed.

Your genes are stored on long threads. Each thread has a cap at each end, like the plastic tip on a shoelace. In many cells the caps get a little shorter every time the cell splits. When they get too short, the cell stops splitting.

Some scientists, like Peter Medawar in 1952 and George Williams in 1957, argued this. Nature mostly shapes how well bodies work while they are young and can have children. So little pushes bodies to stay young for ever.

explanations.art: A shoelace with a plastic tip, drawn next to a long gene thread with glowing caps at both ends that get shorter in three steps.
explanations.context: This card is about one of the big open questions of this unit: why bodies get old at all.

explanations.definition: Death is when a body stops working for good. It is the last stage of every life cycle, for plants, animals and people.
explanations.description: Most people die when they are very old, after a long life. A very old body becomes tired, and its parts slowly stop working. Sometimes people die younger, because of an illness or an accident. That is rare, and doctors work hard to stop it. When a person has died, their pain, cold and hunger are over. It is natural to feel very sad when someone dies. That sadness is a sign of love. People remember those who have died through stories, photos, food they liked and festivals. Different families believe different things about what happens after death. You can ask your family what they believe.
examples: Dry leaves fall from a tree and turn into soil that feeds new plants.
Many Indian families remember their elders on special days, by cooking their favourite food.
The atoms in a body that has died go back into the soil and air, and become part of new living things.
explanations.art: A family sitting together looking through an old photo album, one child pointing at a smiling old man in a photo.
explanations.context: This card talks gently about the end of a life, the last stage of every life cycle. A grown-up may want to read it with the child.

explanations.concept: Why do humans live long after having children? The grandmother idea
explanations.description: Most animals die soon after they stop having babies. Humans, and a few kinds of whales, often live for many years after. Why? Scientists argue about this.
examples: The Hadza people in Tanzania are hunters and gatherers. Grandmothers there dig up many tubers, a kind of root, to feed their grandchildren.
Killer whales are big dolphins. Old grandmother killer whales often lead their family to salmon, especially when food is hard to find.
In many Indian homes, grandparents cook, tell stories and look after children while parents work.

perspectives.explanation: Grandmothers helped feed and care for their grandchildren. So families with long-lived grandmothers had more children who survived. Over many generations, humans came to live longer.
Long life may have come for other reasons, like hunting, sharing skills or bigger brains. The grandmother effect may be real but too small to explain everything.

explanations.art: A grandmother killer whale leading a small family of whales through blue water towards a shoal of silver salmon.
explanations.context: This card is about a big question: why humans live for so many years after they stop having babies.

explanations.concept: People are living longer than ever before
explanations.definition: Life expectancy is how long people are expected to live on average. In India it has more than doubled in about 70 years.
explanations.description: In 1951, a baby born in India could expect to live about 32 years on average. Today it is about 70 years. That does not mean people were old at 32. Back then, many babies and children died of illnesses like cholera and measles. Those early deaths pulled the average down. Clean water, vaccines, better food and doctors changed that. The longest life ever checked with proper records belonged to Jeanne Calment of France. She lived to 122 years, from 1875 to 1997.
examples: Your great-grandparents may have had brothers or sisters who died as babies. Ask your family.
Vaccines given to babies at Indian health centres protect them from illnesses that once killed many.
There are now more people over 60 in India than ever before.
explanations.art: Two bars side by side, a short bar labelled India 1951 about 32 years and a tall bar labelled India today about 70 years, with a water tap and a vaccine bottle beside the tall bar.
explanations.context: This card explains why people in India and the world live longer than people did long ago.

explanations.concept: Can ageing be slowed? The frontier
explanations.description: Some living things barely seem to age. Scientists study them to learn how ageing works. Nobody yet knows how to stop human ageing, and some think we never will.
examples: In 1993, Cynthia Kenyon changed one gene in tiny worms. The worms lived about twice as long.
Tiny water animals called hydras showed no signs of ageing in a four-year study by Daniel Martínez in 1998.
Greenland sharks swim in icy seas. Scientists in 2016 found one that was at least 272 years old.

perspectives.explanation: Ageing is a set of changes we can learn to slow, like slowing an illness. One day people may stay healthy much longer.
Human bodies may have a natural limit of about 120 years. Helping people stay healthy and active until the end matters more than living for ever.

explanations.art: A tiny see-through hydra with waving arms beside a huge slow Greenland shark in dark icy water.
explanations.context: This card is about what scientists are still finding out: whether ageing could be slowed down.

agreed.text: Every human goes through the same life stages, in the same order.
agreed.evidence: Doctors have measured and recorded millions of babies, children and adults all over the world. Everyone grows and changes in the same order, though at slightly different speeds.

agreed.text: Babies and young children grow faster than at any other time.
agreed.evidence: Height charts used in every Indian health centre show a baby grows about 25 centimetres in its first year, but a child grows only about 5 to 6 centimetres a year.

agreed.text: Grey hair, wrinkles and needing reading glasses are normal parts of ageing.
agreed.evidence: These changes are seen in people everywhere. Scientists can see the causes under microscopes: fewer pigment cells in hair roots, fewer springy threads in skin and stiffer eye lenses.

agreed.text: The body keeps making new cells all through life.
agreed.evidence: Scientists can count and date cells. Red blood cells last about four months, and the outer skin is replaced about every month.

agreed.text: Exercise, good food, sleep and friends help people stay healthy at every age.
agreed.evidence: Large studies that follow thousands of people for many years find that active people with friends usually stay stronger and healthier for longer.

agreed.text: People in India and the world live much longer now than 100 years ago.
agreed.evidence: Birth and death records show life expectancy in India rose from about 32 years in 1951 to about 70 years today.

challenging.claim: Old people cannot learn new things.
challenging.who: A common belief. Many people think this without checking.
challenging.for: Learning very fast things, like a new video game, often does get slower with age.
challenging.against: Brains keep making new connections all life long. In 2018, Karthyayani Amma of Kerala passed a literacy exam at 96. Man Kaur of Chandigarh started running races in her nineties and won medals.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea about older people, and why the evidence says it is wrong.

challenging.claim: Every cell in your body is replaced every seven years.
challenging.who: A popular saying, repeated in many books and websites.
challenging.for: Many cells really are replaced, and some, like skin and blood, are replaced much faster than seven years.
challenging.against: There is no seven-year rule. Gut cells are replaced in days. Most brain cells and the cells in the middle of your eye lens are never replaced. Scientists checked this by measuring the age of cells in 2005.
challenging.context: This card is about a popular saying about our cells, and what scientists found when they checked.

challenging.claim: Worry and fright can turn hair grey.
challenging.who: An old saying in many countries. Stories tell of people going grey overnight after a shock.
challenging.for: In 2020, a team led by Ya-Chieh Hsu found that great stress in mice used up the cells that make hair colour. The mice went grey.
challenging.against: Hair that has already grown cannot change colour overnight. Stress may make new hair grow in grey sooner, but genes and age matter most. More studies in humans are needed.
challenging.context: This card is about the old idea that worry makes hair grey, and what scientists have found so far.

challenging.claim: Ageing is an illness that doctors could one day cure.
challenging.who: Some scientists who study ageing, and some companies that sell anti-ageing products.
challenging.for: Scientists have made worms, flies and mice live much longer by changing genes or food. Some animals barely seem to age.
challenging.against: Many scientists say ageing is not one illness but many slow changes at once. No product has been shown to stop ageing in humans. The oldest people still die at around 110 to 120.
challenging.context: This card is about a big argument among scientists: can ageing be cured?

challenging.claim: Adult brains never make any new brain cells.
challenging.who: Most scientists believed this for much of the 1900s.
challenging.for: Most brain cells we have as adults were made before we were born or as babies.
challenging.against: Studies since the 1990s found new brain cells being made in one part of the adult brain, used for memory. Scientists still argue how many are made in old age.
challenging.context: This card is about whether grown-up and older brains can make new brain cells.

challenging.claim: Elders are a burden, and young people do all the useful work.
challenging.who: An attitude some people have, though few say it aloud.
challenging.for: Some elders need a lot of care, especially when they are ill.
challenging.against: Elders care for grandchildren, cook, teach, keep family memories and give advice. The grandmother idea says long-lived grandmothers helped human children survive. In killer whales, old grandmothers lead their families to food.
challenging.context: This card is about how we think of older people, and what the evidence shows about the help they give.

big_questions.q: Your grandparent was once a baby. Is the baby and the grandparent the same person? What stayed the same?
big_questions.hint: Think about what changed: size, skin, hair, cells. Now think about what might not have changed.

big_questions.q: If most of your cells are replaced, why do you still remember things from when you were four?
big_questions.hint: Most cells in the thinking part of your brain stay with you all your life.

big_questions.q: Would you want to live for ever? What would be good about it, and what might be hard?
big_questions.hint: Think about friends, the Earth, new babies being born, and what makes days special.

big_questions.q: Why does a mouse live about 2 years, and a human about 80?
big_questions.hint: Their cells are very alike. So what might be different? Think about genes, size and danger.

big_questions.q: What can an elder do better than you? What can you do better than an elder?
big_questions.hint: Think about eyes, ears and legs. Then think about stories, skills and patience.

big_questions.q: How should a family, a town or a country take care of its elders?
big_questions.hint: Think about ramps, big-print signs, seats on buses, and who visits them.

big_questions.q: If you could look at your own hands at 80, what do you think they will look like? What will they know how to do?
big_questions.hint: Hands that have cooked, written or played music for 70 years learn a lot.

big_questions.q: Is ageing something that happens to us, or something we are doing all the time?
big_questions.hint: Remember that your body makes about 4 million new cells every second.

big_questions.q: When someone dies, where do the atoms of their body go?
big_questions.hint: Think of a fallen leaf turning into soil, and a new plant growing from it.

big_questions.q: Why do we feel sad when someone we love dies? What does the sadness tell us?
big_questions.hint: We do not miss people we never cared about.

story.title: The Needle Who Knew Two Hands
story.note: Chikankari, the white-thread embroidery of Lucknow, is real, and so are the lanes of Chowk where it is sewn. Rahmat Chacha, Zoya and the needle are made up.
text: I am a needle. I am thin and silver, as long as your little finger. I have lived for sixty years in the cap of Rahmat Chacha, in a narrow lane in the old part of Lucknow.

When Rahmat first held me, he was eight years old. His fingers were small and quick. His eyes were sharp as a sparrow's. He held the cloth so close to his face that his nose almost touched it. He threaded me in one try, every time, and laughed at the grown-ups who squinted.

His teacher was an old woman called Bano Apa. She held the cloth far away, at the end of her long arms. 'My arms have grown too short,' she used to say. Rahmat thought it was a joke. He did not understand it. Not then.

Rahmat grew. His voice cracked and dropped. He grew tall. His fingers got long and strong. Together we made a hundred kurtas, then a thousand. We made white flowers on white cloth, so fine that you had to tilt it to the light to see them. That is chikankari. It is a slow, patient kind of sewing.

The years went by like threads through cloth. His black hair turned to salt and pepper, then to salt. Little lines grew at the corners of his eyes, in the places where he smiled. And slowly, so slowly that he did not notice at first, he began to hold the cloth further away.

One morning, he held me up to the window. He licked the end of the thread. He poked at my eye. He missed. He tried again. He missed again. My eye is the tiny hole at my top, and it had not changed at all. It was his eyes that had changed.
'My arms have grown too short,' he said, and this time he did not laugh.

That was the year Zoya came. She was eight, and she lived two doors down. After school she sat on his step, swinging her legs, and watched. One day he held me out to her. 'Can you?' he asked. She held me close to her nose, the way he once had, and threaded me in one try.

After that she came every day. She threaded six needles for him, one after another, and stuck them in his cap like little flags. In return, he taught her stitches. The shadow stitch. The tiny knot called phanda, round as a mustard seed.
'Why can't you see the hole any more?' she asked him once.

Rahmat tapped the corner of his eye. 'There is a little window in here,' he said, 'that bends to look at near things. When you are young, it is soft, like jelly. Mine has gone stiff, like an old rubber band. Far away, I see the kites over the river. Near, everything is fog.'
Zoya looked at her own hands. 'Will mine go stiff too?'
'If you are lucky,' he said, 'and live long enough.'

Then came the night of the wedding dupatta. It was the hottest week of the summer. A bride's family had ordered a long white dupatta, covered in flowers, for the morning. There were still three flowers to finish. Zoya had threaded a whole row of needles and was sitting with Rahmat by the lamp.
Then the lights went out. The fan creaked to a stop. The whole lane went black. Somewhere a dog barked. Zoya's mother called from the next house that the power would not be back till morning.
Zoya held the cloth up to her face. She could see nothing at all. Not the flowers. Not the cloth. Not me. 'It's ruined,' she whispered. 'We can't see.'
In the dark, Rahmat laughed. It was a soft, surprised laugh. 'Now,' he said, 'we have the same eyes.'

He took the cloth from her. He did not hold it near, and he did not hold it far. He laid it on his knee and closed his eyes. His fingertips moved across it like an ant across a leaf. They found the edge of the last flower. They counted the threads, one, two, three. Then I felt his hand pick me up and push me through, exactly where I needed to go.

For sixty years his eyes had been changing. But all that time his fingers had been learning. They had sewn so many flowers that they could feel where the next stitch belonged. His eyes had grown older. His hands had grown wiser.

'Give me your hand,' he said to Zoya. He put her fingers on the cloth and his own fingers over hers. 'Feel the bump? That is the last knot. Now one thread over. There.' He guided her hand. Together they made one phanda, then another, in the dark.
They sewed like that all night, two hands on one needle. A small soft hand, and a big wrinkled one. I could not tell where one ended and the other began.

When the sky over the river turned grey, the lights flickered back on. Zoya blinked at the cloth. All three flowers were done. Some of the knots were tiny and perfect. A few were a little lumpy. Those were hers. Rahmat said those were his favourites.

I am still a needle. I have been held by a boy who became an old man. Now I am held by a girl who will one day be an old woman. Some days, when she is sewing on his step, I think it is only one hand that holds me. It is just very long, and it reaches all the way across the years.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Rahmat cannot thread the needle because the lens in his eye has stiffened with age. This is presbyopia, and nearly everyone gets it by their mid-forties. The lens never sheds old cells. It keeps adding layers, so it gets thicker and stiffer. Zoya's young lens is soft, so she sees near things sharply. But ageing is not only losing things. While his lens stiffened, his hands were learning, and sixty years of practice let him sew by touch. In the dark, eyes stop mattering and the old man's skill becomes the key.
ask: In the story, why could Rahmat Chacha not thread the needle any more? Was something wrong with the needle?
Why could Zoya thread it in one try?
When the lights went out, why did Rahmat say they now had 'the same eyes'?
What had Rahmat's hands been learning while his eyes were getting older?
At the end, the needle says it feels held by 'one hand' that reaches across the years. What do you think it means?

Rahmat as an old man with white hair, holding a needle up to the window light and squinting, the thread missing the eye.
Zoya sitting on a stone step threading needles and sticking them into an old man's white cap like little flags.

games.title: Who Am I? The Life Stage Game
games.players: 2 to 6 players, or one child playing against the app
games.context: This is a card game about the stages of a human life: baby, child, teenager, adult and older adult. Players read a clue card and decide which stage it describes.

I grew about 25 centimetres this year, the fastest I will ever grow.
My milk teeth are falling out one by one.
I can read tiny print held 10 centimetres from my nose.
I grow about 5 or 6 centimetres every year.
My voice is cracking and getting deeper.
I grew so fast this year that none of my shoes fit.
My growth plates have just closed. I will not grow any taller.
My bones are at their thickest and strongest.
I have started holding the newspaper further away to read it.
I found my first few grey hairs.
My hair is mostly white now.
I hold my phone at arm's length to read a message.
I hear high whistles less well than I used to.
My skin has soft lines where I have smiled for years.
I know the words to songs nobody else in the family remembers.
I have shrunk about 3 centimetres since I was 40.
I do yoga every morning to keep my knees moving.

ALL AGES: I can learn something new today.

ALL AGES: Exercise makes my muscles stronger.

flow.do: 1. Lay the life line mat on the floor. 2. Shuffle the 30 cards and put them face down. 3. Put the star tokens in a bowl.

flow.kid: Lay the mat on the floor. Mix up the cards. Every person goes through these stages. Each card is a clue to one stage.

flow.do: Take turns reading cards and placing them. After each card, ask the player to say why.
flow.say: Read the card out loud. Which stage is it? Tell us why you think so.
flow.kid: Read your card out loud. Which stage is it? Say why.

ask.q: Why does 'My head is one quarter of my whole length' go on BABY?
good: Babies have big heads compared to their bodies.
A grown-up's head is only about one eighth of their length.

flow.parent: Clue cards about reading distance belong to ADULT or OLDER ADULT, since the eye lens stiffens from about 40. Accept either and talk about it.

flow.do: When someone draws an ALL AGES card, stop and talk about it.
flow.say: This one is true for babies, children and grandparents too. Your body is making new cells right now, and so is Nani's.
flow.kid: ALL AGES cards are true for everyone. A baby and a grandparent both do this.

check.q: Which of these is true at EVERY age, from baby to elder?
options: Having a soft spot on the head
check.why: Every living body, young or old, keeps making new cells, millions every second. Fast growing like 25 centimetres a year only happens in the first year. The soft spot on the head closes by about age two.

flow.context: This step of the Life Stage Game is about the cards that are true at every age.

flow.do: When the cards run out, count stars. Then look at the whole mat together.
flow.say: Look at the whole line. You will move along it too. Which stage are you at now? Which stage am I at? Which is the one you are most curious about?
flow.kid: Count your stars. Look at the whole line. Find where you are now. Where will you be one day?
flow.think: Every elder on this mat was once a baby. Is a baby and an elder the same person?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Life Stage Game. You count stars and look at the whole life line.

games.context: This is a board game like snakes and ladders. Each square is one year of a life, from 1 to 100. Ladders are habits that help a body at every age. Slides are things that harm it.

flow.kid: Every square is one year of life. You start as a baby at square 1. Ladders help your body. Slides harm it.

check.q: On the board, a ladder goes from 63 to 84 for doing strength exercises. What have scientists found about exercise in old age?
options: It is too late to get stronger after 60
Muscles can get stronger at any age, even at 90
check.why: In 1990, scientists gave strength exercises to people of about 90, and their muscles got much stronger in eight weeks. Picking 'too late' is a common belief, but the evidence shows bodies keep responding to exercise all life long.
