items.p: Put these life stages in order, from first to last: adult, baby, older adult, teenager, child.
items: baby
child
teenager
adult
older adult
items.a: order shown
items.why: Every person goes through the stages in this order. Nobody skips one, and nobody goes backwards.

items.p: When does a person grow fastest?
opts: In the first year of life
Everyone grows at the same speed all life
items.why: A baby grows from about 50 to about 75 centimetres in its first year. That is faster than any other time. Picking 'the same speed' usually means growth has been pictured as steady, but it comes in fast and slow times.

items.p: A baby in its first year of life is called an ____.
items.why: An infant is a baby in its first year.

items.p: A baby's head is bigger compared to its body than an adult's head is.
items.why: True. A baby's head is about one quarter of its length. An adult's head is only about one eighth.

items.p: Why does hair turn grey or white?
opts: The cells at the hair root stop making colour
The sun bleaches the hair inside the head
items.why: Pigment cells at the root put colour into each new hair. As they run out, new hair grows white. Picking 'overnight' is a common story, but hair that has already grown cannot change colour.

items.p: Why does older skin get wrinkles?
opts: It has fewer springy threads, and gets thinner and drier
Wrinkles come from washing too much
items.why: Skin has springy threads called collagen and elastin. The body makes fewer of them as we age, so skin folds instead of bouncing back. Picking 'thicker' is the opposite of what happens.

items.p: The clear, bendy part inside the eye that helps us focus is called the ____.
items.why: The lens changes shape to focus on near or far things.

items.p: Most people need reading glasses by about age 45, because the lens in the eye gets stiffer.
items.why: True. A stiffer lens cannot focus on close things, so small print looks blurry.

items.p: Match each life stage to something that often happens in it.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each stage has its own changes. Babies learn to walk, children lose milk teeth, teenagers grow fast, adults are strongest, and elders' hair often turns white.

items.p: Sort these. Do they usually get HARDER or can they get BETTER with age?
items: reading tiny print
Often gets harder
knowing many words
Can get better
hearing very high sounds
Often gets harder
telling family stories
Can get better
running fast
Often gets harder
knowing what to do in a crisis
Can get better
items.a: see items
items.why: Bodies slow down with age, but knowledge, words and experience can keep growing all life.

items.p: Remember the snap-back skin test, where you gently pinched the back of a hand? Write what happened to an older person's skin compared to yours.
items.a: The older person's skin took longer to go flat. Mine went flat in less than 1 second. Theirs took about 3 seconds. Older skin has fewer springy threads.
items.why: Older skin has less collagen and elastin, so it springs back more slowly.

items.p: Your body makes millions of new cells every second. Which part is NOT replaced during your life?
opts: The cells in the middle of the eye lens
items.why: The cells in the middle of your eye lens were made before you were born and stay all your life. Skin, blood and gut lining are replaced again and again. Picking 'skin' usually means it has been pictured as fixed, but outer skin is replaced about every month.

items.p: Muscles cannot get stronger after age 60.
items.why: False. In 1990, people aged about 90 got much stronger muscles after eight weeks of strength exercise. Muscles respond to exercise at any age.

items.p: Draw the same person at three ages: 5, 35 and 75. Show at least three body changes.
items.a: A small child with a big head and milk teeth, a tall adult, and an older person with grey hair, some wrinkles and reading glasses.
items.why: Bodies change in size, proportion, hair, skin and eyes over a lifetime.

items.p: Name two ways you could help an elder in your home or neighbourhood.
items.a: I could carry their bag. I could read small print for them. I could put a rubber mat in the bathroom.
items.why: Good help fits the changes in older bodies: eyes, grip, balance and bones. Always ask first if they want help.

items.p: When a living thing's body stops working for good, we say it has ____. It is the last stage of every life cycle.
items.why: Death is the last stage of every life cycle, for plants, animals and people.

items.p: Remember the near point test, where people brought tiny print closer until it blurred? A child read it at 8 cm and a grandfather at 60 cm. What does this show?
opts: The eye lens gets stiffer with age
items.why: In a fair test everyone used the same card. The grandfather's stiffer lens cannot focus up close. Picking 'longer arms' is the joke elders make, but arm length is not the cause.

items.p: In the high sound test, who is most likely to hear a sound of 15,000 hertz?
items.why: Hair cells for very high sounds wear out first with age, so young ears hear the highest sounds. Picking 'the same' means hearing has been pictured as fixed.

items.p: Every cell in your body is replaced exactly every seven years.
items.why: False. There is no seven-year rule. Gut cells are replaced in days, skin in about a month, and some brain and eye lens cells never.

items.p: A red blood cell lives for about ____ months.
items.why: Red blood cells last about 120 days, which is about four months.

items.p: In 1951, life expectancy in India was about 32 years. Why was it so low?
opts: Many babies and children died of illnesses, which pulled the average down
items.why: An average counts every life, including the many babies who died of illnesses like cholera. Picking 'everyone was old at 32' is a common mistake. Many people then lived to 60 or 70.

items.p: Match the scientist to the discovery.
pairs: found telomerase, which rebuilds the caps on genes
found cells in a dish stop splitting after 40 to 60 times
made worms live twice as long by changing one gene
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These scientists each helped us understand ageing. Blackburn, Greider and Kenyon are among the women who led this science.

items.p: Why do many elders walk carefully on wet floors?
opts: Bones get thinner with age, so a fall can break one
Elders cannot walk fast at all
Wet floors are only slippery for elders
items.why: Bones lose some hard minerals with age and can break in a fall. Picking 'cannot walk fast at all' is a belief about elders that is often wrong.

items.p: Give one thing that gets harder with age, and one thing that can get better. Explain each.
items.a: Reading tiny print gets harder, because the eye lens gets stiffer. Knowing words can get better, because we keep learning new words all our lives.
items.why: Ageing is not only losing. Some abilities slow down, but knowledge and experience can keep growing.

items.p: Sort these by how often the body replaces them.
items: gut lining
Every few days or weeks
outer skin
Every few days or weeks
red blood cells
Every few months or years
bones
Every few months or years
middle of the eye lens
Never, they stay all life
most brain cells
Never, they stay all life
items.a: see items
items.why: Different parts of the body renew at very different speeds. So you are partly new and partly as old as you are.

items.p: What is the longest human lifespan that has been checked with proper records?
items.why: Jeanne Calment of France lived 122 years, from 1875 to 1997. Stories of people living 200 years or more have no proper records.

items.p: A hair that has already grown can turn white overnight from a shock.
items.why: False. A hair that has grown cannot change colour. Stress may make new hairs grow in grey sooner, which scientists are still studying.

items.p: Why do scientists ask everyone to use the same card in the near point test?
items.a: So that only the person's age changes. If the print were bigger for some people, the test would not be fair.
items.why: A fair test changes only one thing at a time.

items.p: What is the 'grandmother idea'?
opts: Grandmothers who helped feed grandchildren helped humans evolve longer lives
items.why: Kristen Hawkes and her team suggested in 1998 that grandmothers' help let more children survive. It is debated, and other scientists suggest other reasons.

items.p: The closest distance at which you can still see something sharply is called your near ____.
items.why: The near point moves further away as the eye lens stiffens with age.

items.p: Draw an eye from the side with a soft, round lens for a child and a flatter, stiffer lens for an elder. Show a book close to each eye. Is it sharp or blurry?
items.a: The child's round lens makes the close book sharp. The elder's stiff lens makes the close book blurry.
items.why: A soft lens can bulge to focus on near things. A stiff one cannot.
items.art: Two empty side views of eyes.

items.p: Your body makes about 4 million new cells every second. Is it still the same body as last year? Give reasons for your answer.
items.a: Any thoughtful answer. For example: Much of it is new, because skin, blood and gut cells have been replaced. But some cells, like brain and eye lens cells, are the same. And the pattern of my body, and my memories, carry on. So it is the same body, but rebuilt.
items.why: This is a real puzzle that thinkers have argued about for thousands of years. Good answers use the facts about cell renewal.

items.p: Scientists argue about why bodies age. Which of these is NOT one of their main ideas?
opts: Bodies age because birthdays make them older
Small damage builds up faster than it is repaired
The caps on the ends of genes get shorter
Nature mostly shapes how bodies work while young
items.why: Birthdays only count the years. They do not cause ageing. The other three are real scientific ideas, and many scientists think more than one is true.

items.p: A mouse lives about 2 years. A human lives about 80. Their cells are very alike. Suggest one reason for the difference.
items.a: Their genes may set a different timetable. Or a mouse is eaten by cats and owls so young that nature never shaped it to live long. Humans are protected and cared for, so long life helped.
items.why: This is an open question. Scientists point to genes, size, and how dangerous an animal's life is.

items.p: Killer whale grandmothers often lead their families to salmon. Which idea does this support?
opts: Elders can help their families survive
items.why: Grandmother killer whales remember where food is, especially in hard years. This supports the idea that long life after having babies can help a family.

items.p: Some scientists say ageing is an illness that may one day be cured. Others disagree. What do you think? Give one reason.
items.a: Any reasoned answer. For example: I think we can slow it, because scientists made worms live twice as long. Or: I think it cannot be cured, because ageing is many changes at once.
items.why: This is debated. A good answer gives a reason and uses evidence.

items.p: Life expectancy of 32 years in 1951 means most people in India died at 32.
items.why: False. An average includes the many babies who died very young. Many people who survived childhood lived into their sixties and seventies.

items.p: Telomeres are caps on the ends of the threads that hold your genes. They are often compared to what?
items.why: Like a shoelace tip stops fraying, a telomere protects the end of the gene thread. In many cells it gets shorter each time the cell splits.

items.p: Remember the snap-back skin test? The results can change if someone has drunk very little water. How would you make the test fairer?
items.a: Ask everyone to drink a glass of water an hour before. Test everyone at the same time of day.
items.why: Good scientists look for other things that could change the result, and keep them the same.

items.p: When a body dies, its atoms go back into soil, water and air. Where might they go next?
items.a: Into a plant, which a cow or a person might eat. Into a tree. Into a river. Into a new living thing.
items.why: Atoms are never lost. They move through the soil, plants and animals again and again.

items.p: Grandma's outer skin was made in the last few weeks. The middle of her eye lens was made before she was born. What does this show?
opts: One body has parts of many different ages
The eye lens is replaced every week
items.why: Skin is replaced again and again, but the lens keeps its oldest cells all life. So one body holds parts that are a few weeks old and parts older than the person.

items.p: Design a sign for a bus that would help elders. What would it say, and how would it look?
items.a: A big sign in dark letters on a light background that says 'Seats for elders'. With a picture, so people who cannot read can understand it.
items.why: Good design fits changes in older eyes: big, dark letters with strong contrast are easier to read.

items.p: Hydras are tiny water animals. In a 1998 study, they showed no signs of ageing for four years. What does this tell scientists?
opts: Ageing is not the same for every living thing
Hydras live for ever, for sure
items.why: Hydras seem to keep renewing their bodies. This shows ageing is not fixed for all life. Scientists still do not know if hydras truly never age.

items.p: Why do we feel sad when someone dies? How do people in your family remember those who have died?
items.a: Any honest answer. For example: We feel sad because we loved them and miss them. My family lights a lamp and cooks their favourite food on their day.
items.why: Grief is a sign of love. Families and cultures have many ways of remembering.

items.p: Sort these claims about ageing.
items: Bodies go through stages in the same order
Scientists agree
Exercise helps at any age
Scientists agree
Why bodies age at all
Scientists still argue
Whether ageing can be cured
Scientists still argue
Grey hair comes from fewer pigment cells
Scientists agree
How many new brain cells old brains make
Scientists still argue
items.a: see items
items.why: Science is sure about many facts of ageing, but its deepest causes are still open.

items.p: Write a short letter to yourself at age 80. What do you hope your body and mind will be like?
items.a: Any thoughtful letter that mentions some body changes and some things that grow with age, like knowledge or friendships.
items.why: Imagining your own old age helps you see elders as people who were once just like you.

experiments.title: The Snap-Back Skin Test
experiments.question: Does skin spring back more slowly as people get older?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Whose skin will go flat fastest after a gentle pinch? Line up the people you will test, from the one you think is fastest to the one you think is slowest. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, keep everything the same except the person's age. Pinch the same place, the back of the hand. Pinch for the same time, 3 seconds. Keep the hand flat on the table. Test each person 3 times, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: a clock or phone with a seconds timer, or count 'one mango, two mango'
3 to 5 people of different ages, who say yes to being tested
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Pinch very gently, only the loose skin on the back of the hand. Always ask first. Stop if anyone says it hurts. Never laugh at anyone's skin.

schedule.what: Guess. Test each person 3 times. Write down the seconds. Then draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart. Draw one bar for each person, in order of age. Make each bar as tall as that person's middle value.
experiments.context: This is the snap-back skin test. You gently pinch the skin on the back of a hand for 3 seconds, let go, and count how long the skin takes to go flat. You compare people of different ages.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: seconds for pinched skin to go flat
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A hand resting flat on a table, palm down, with two fingers gently pinching a small fold of skin on the back.
setup.caption: 1. Gently pinch the skin on the back of the hand for 3 seconds.

setup.art: The fingers letting go, and a small ridge of skin standing up, with a phone timer beside the hand.
setup.caption: 2. Let go and start counting.

setup.art: The same hand with smooth flat skin again and the timer stopped, a child writing a number in a table.
setup.caption: 3. Stop when the skin is flat. Write down the seconds.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess, and to line up the people from fastest to slowest.
flow.say: We will gently pinch the skin on the back of a hand, let go, and count until it goes flat. Whose skin do you think will go flat fastest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: We will pinch skin gently and see how fast it goes flat. Guess whose skin is fastest. Line everyone up, fastest to slowest. Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of the snap-back skin test. Here you guess what will happen before testing.

flow.do: Show how to pinch gently on your own hand first.
flow.say: Let's practise on my hand first. Rest it flat. Pinch only the loose skin, softly, like picking up a feather. Hold it while we count to three. Then let go.
flow.kid: Practise on your own hand. Rest it flat. Pinch the loose skin very softly. Count to three. Let go.
flow.parent: Show that it does not hurt. Ask each person's permission before you pinch them. This teaches that we ask before touching anyone's body.
flow.context: This step of the snap-back skin test shows how to pinch gently and safely.

flow.do: 1. Test each person 3 times on the back of the hand. 2. Time from letting go until the skin is flat. 3. Write each time in the table.
flow.say: Ready, pinch, one, two, three, let go. Watch the little ridge of skin. Say stop when it is flat.
flow.kid: Ask first. Pinch for three seconds. Let go. Count until the skin is flat. Write the number. Do it 3 times.
flow.parent: Young skin goes flat almost at once, so write 'less than 1 second'. Skin of people over 60 can stay up for a few seconds. Between a child and a parent of 35 there may be almost no difference, so test an elder if you can, such as a grandparent or an older neighbour. Drinking little water can also slow it down, so it is not a perfect test.
flow.context: This is the main step of the snap-back skin test. You test each person 3 times and write down the seconds.

flow.do: For each person, find the middle value of the three tries.
flow.say: Put the three numbers in order, smallest to biggest. The one in the middle is the middle value. It is a fair number to use, because it ignores one very fast or very slow try.
flow.kid: Put the 3 numbers in order. The middle one is the one we use.

check.q: Arjun, a boy in Class 3, did the skin test with his Nani, his mother's mother. Her three tries took 2, 5 and 3 seconds. What is the middle value?
check.why: In order, the numbers are 2, 3, 5. The middle one is 3. Picking 5 usually means taking the biggest number. Picking 2 means taking the smallest. The middle value is fairer, because one odd try does not change it.

flow.context: This step of the snap-back skin test is about finding the middle value of three tries.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: older skin springs back more slowly. What I saw: my skin went flat in less than 1 second, but Nani's took 3 seconds. Why: older skin has fewer springy threads inside.
flow.context: This is the last step of the snap-back skin test. Your child explains the result.

experiments.title: How Close Can You Read?
experiments.question: Does the closest distance at which people can read clearly change with age?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Who in your family can read tiny print closest to their nose? Who will need it furthest away? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use the same card with the same tiny print for everyone. Test in the same bright room. Everyone uses both eyes. Someone who wears reading glasses only for reading takes them off. Someone who wears glasses all day for seeing far keeps them on. Test each person 3 times, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: a card or medicine packet with a line of very small print. Use the same one for everyone.
a 30 cm school ruler or a tailor's tape. For longer distances, hold a piece of string from cheek to card, then measure the string.
3 to 5 people of different ages. A child and one grown-up over 40 is enough to see a difference.
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Never touch the eye with the card or ruler. Hold the end of the tape against the cheekbone, not the eye.

schedule.what: Guess. Measure each person's closest sharp reading distance 3 times. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart, one bar for each person in order of age.
experiments.context: This is the near point test. A person holds a card with tiny print at arm's length, then slowly brings it closer. When the letters go blurry, you measure the distance from the card to their face.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: closest distance at which tiny print looks sharp
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A child holding a small card with tiny print at arm's length, looking at it.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the card with tiny print at arm's length.

setup.art: The same child slowly bringing the card towards the face, the letters starting to blur.
setup.caption: 2. Bring it slowly closer until the letters go blurry.

setup.art: A parent holding the end of a measuring tape against the child's cheekbone and the other end at the card.
setup.caption: 3. Move it back until sharp again. Measure from face to card.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess who can read tiny print closest.
flow.say: Some grown-ups hold a phone far away to read it. Let's measure how close each person in our family can hold tiny print and still read it. Who do you think can hold it closest? Who will need it furthest away? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Some grown-ups hold a phone far away to read it. Guess who can read tiny print closest to their nose. Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of the near point test. You guess who can read tiny print closest to their face.

flow.do: 1. The person holds the card at arm's length. 2. They bring it slowly towards their face. 3. When the letters blur, they move it back a little until it is just sharp. 4. Measure from cheekbone to card. 5. Repeat 3 times for each person.
flow.say: Bring it closer, slowly. Tell me the moment the letters go fuzzy. Now move it back just until they are sharp. Hold still while I measure.
flow.kid: Hold the card far away. Bring it closer slowly. Stop when the letters go fuzzy. Move it back until sharp. Measure.
flow.parent: Children often reach 7 to 10 centimetres. People over 45 without reading glasses often need 30 centimetres or more. If an elder cannot see the print sharply even at arm's length, write 'more than arm's length'. A short-sighted person without their glasses can read very close at any age. That is why they keep their glasses on.
flow.context: This is the main step of the near point test. You measure how close each person can hold tiny print and still read it.

flow.do: Look at the bars together.
flow.say: Look at the bars. What happens to the distance as people get older?
flow.kid: Look at your bars. What happens as people get older?

check.q: In the near point test, a grandmother of 58 needed the card 60 centimetres away. A child of 8 could read it at 8 centimetres. Why?
options: The grandmother's eye lens has got stiffer, so it cannot focus on near things
The grandmother's eyes have got smaller
check.why: The lens in an older eye gets stiffer, so it cannot bulge enough to focus on close things. Far-away things can still look sharp. Picking 'eyes got smaller' is a common guess, but eyes stay about the same size all adult life.

flow.context: This step of the near point test asks your child to explain the results.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences: what I think, what I saw, why.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: older people need to hold small print further away. What I saw: I could read at 8 centimetres, but Dadaji needed 60 centimetres. Why: the lens in his eye has got stiff, so it cannot focus up close.
flow.context: This is the last step of the near point test. Your child explains what they found.

experiments.title: The Mosquito Sound
experiments.question: Can younger people hear higher sounds than older people?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Who will hear the highest sound? Will anyone hear sounds the others cannot? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, play every sound from the same speaker, at the same quiet volume, from the same distance. Everyone sits in the same quiet room. Each person raises a hand when they hear a sound, without looking at the screen.

materials.item: a phone or computer with an online tone generator
3 to 5 people of different ages
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: A grown-up controls the volume. Keep it quiet, never loud. Never use earphones for this test. Stop at once if a sound feels uncomfortable.

schedule.what: Guess. Play four high sounds quietly. Write who heard each one.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a tick for each sound a person heard. Then colour in a bar for each person up to their highest sound.
experiments.context: This is the high sound test. A grown-up plays quiet beeps that get higher and higher. Everyone raises a hand when they hear one. You find the highest sound each person can hear.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: the highest sound each person heard
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Phone speakers may not play the very highest sounds.

setup.art: A family sitting in a quiet room with eyes closed, a phone on a table showing a simple tone generator screen.
setup.caption: 1. Everyone sits quietly. A grown-up sets the volume low.

setup.art: A parent tapping the phone screen while a child raises a hand and a grandfather does not.
setup.caption: 2. Play each sound. Raise your hand if you hear it.

setup.art: A child ticking boxes in a table with columns for each sound.
setup.caption: 3. Tick who heard each sound.

flow.do: 1. Open an online tone generator. 2. Set the volume low. 3. Set it to 4,000 hertz, a medium-high beep.
flow.say: Sounds can be low, like a drum, or high, like a whistle. How high a sound is, is measured in hertz. Let's see who can hear the highest sounds.
flow.kid: Fetch a grown-up for this test. Sounds can be low or high. We will play higher and higher beeps.
flow.parent: Hertz means how many times a second the air vibrates, or shakes back and forth. 4,000 hertz is a sharp beep. Young children can often hear up to about 17,000 hertz or more. Many older people hear only up to 8,000 to 10,000.
flow.context: This is the first step of the high sound test. A grown-up gets the tone generator ready.

flow.do: Play 4,000, then 8,000, then 12,000, then 15,000 hertz for 3 seconds each. Keep the volume the same. Write a tick for everyone who raises a hand.
flow.say: Eyes closed. Raise your hand if you hear anything.
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Raise your hand when you hear a beep. Write a tick for each person.
flow.parent: Some phone speakers cannot play the highest sounds. If nobody hears 15,000, that may be the phone, not the ears.
flow.context: This is the main step of the high sound test. You play four sounds and see who hears each one.

flow.do: Look at the table together.
flow.say: Who heard the highest sound? Why do you think older ears miss them?
flow.kid: Who heard the highest beep? Why might older ears miss it?

check.q: Priya, a girl in Class 3, played beeps to her family. She heard a beep of 15,000 hertz. Her grandfather did not. What is the best reason?
options: The tiny hair cells for high sounds wear out first as we age
High sounds are too quiet for anyone over 10
check.why: Deep inside the ear are tiny hair cells that pick up sounds. The ones for very high sounds wear out first over the years. Picking 'not listening' blames the person, but this happens to almost everyone as they age.

flow.context: This step of the high sound test asks your child to explain the results.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences: what I think, what I saw, why.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think? What did you see? Why?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: young people can hear higher sounds. What I saw: I heard 15,000 hertz but Nana only heard up to 8,000. Why: the hair cells for high sounds in his ears have worn out over the years.
flow.context: This is the last step of the high sound test. Your child explains what they found.

activities.title: Hands Across Time

materials.item: the hands of people of different ages, or photos of hands
a sheet of paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Ask each person before you touch their hand.

schedule.what: Compare hands of different ages. Say what you notice and wonder.

activities.record: Draw around your hand and an elder's hand on one sheet. Write three things you noticed.
activities.context: This is a noticing activity to start the unit. You look closely at the hands of people of different ages and say what you notice and what you wonder.

setup.art: Three hands laid flat side by side on a table: a child's, a parent's and a grandparent's.
setup.caption: 1. Lay hands of different ages side by side.

setup.art: A child looking closely at a grandmother's hand, seeing soft lines and veins.
setup.caption: 2. Look closely. What do you notice?

setup.art: Two hand outlines drawn on paper, a small one inside a bigger one, with notes around them.
setup.caption: 3. Draw around both hands and write what you noticed.

flow.do: 1. Lay your hands flat next to your child's, and an elder's if possible. 2. Look in silence for one minute.
flow.say: Let's just look for one minute, without talking. Then tell me what you notice. There are no wrong answers.
flow.kid: Put your hand next to a grown-up's hand. Look for one minute. What do you notice?

good: My hand is smaller and smoother.
Was her hand like mine once?

flow.parent: Do not explain anything yet. The aim is for questions to come from your child. Write their 'I wonder' questions down to come back to.
flow.context: This is the first step of Hands Across Time. You look at hands of different ages and say what you notice.

flow.do: Draw around both hands on one sheet. Write three noticings next to them.
flow.say: Every hand here was once a baby's hand. Let's draw around them and write down what we noticed. We will find out why during this unit.
flow.kid: Draw around your hand and a grown-up's hand. Write three things you noticed.
flow.think: Grandma's hand was once smaller than yours. When did it change?
flow.context: This is the last step of Hands Across Time. You draw around hands and write what you noticed.

activities.title: Interview an Elder

materials.item: an elder you know: a grandparent, an older neighbour or a family friend, in person or on a phone call
a notebook and pencil, or a phone to record with permission

activities.safety: Only visit elders you and your family know. A grown-up arranges the visit or call.

schedule.what: Ask an elder about how their body and life have changed. Write or draw their answers.

activities.record: Write or draw three of the elder's answers. Add one thing that surprised you.
activities.context: In this activity you interview an elder about their life: what their body could do when they were 8, what has changed, and what has got better.

setup.art: A child sitting cross-legged in front of a grandfather on a charpai, holding a notebook and pencil.
setup.caption: 1. Sit with an elder, in person or on a call.

setup.art: The grandfather talking and moving his hands, and the child writing quickly.
setup.caption: 2. Ask your questions and listen.

setup.art: A notebook page with a drawing of the grandfather as a boy flying a kite, and writing beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Write or draw three answers.

flow.do: Choose five questions together from this list. What games did you play at 8? What could your body do then that it cannot now? What can you do now that you could not do then? When did you get your first grey hair? What is the best thing about being older?
flow.say: Elders are living libraries. They remember things nobody else does. Let's pick five questions to ask.
flow.kid: Elders remember a lot. Pick five questions to ask an elder.
flow.context: This is the first step of Interview an Elder. You choose your questions.

flow.do: Ask the questions, one at a time. Let the elder talk. Write short notes.
flow.say: Listen carefully. If something is interesting, ask, 'Tell me more about that.'
flow.kid: Ask one question at a time. Listen. If you like an answer, say 'Tell me more.' Write short notes.
flow.parent: Many elders love being asked. Some may get emotional talking about people who have died. That is fine. Let your child see that remembering is a kind of love.
flow.context: This is the main step of Interview an Elder. You ask your questions and listen.

flow.do: Talk about what your child learned.
flow.say: What surprised you? Did their body change in the ways we have been learning about?
flow.kid: What surprised you? Did their body change like we learned?

check.q: In your interview, an elder says, 'At your age I could thread a needle easily. Now I need glasses.' Which change in the body does that show?
options: The lens in the eye getting stiffer
check.why: As people age, the lens in the eye gets stiffer, so close things like a needle's eye look blurry. Bones stop getting longer after the teenage years, and milk teeth fall out in childhood, so those do not fit an elder.

flow.context: This is the last step of Interview an Elder. You talk about what you learned.

activities.title: Life Stage Parade

materials.item: some open floor space
music, if you like

activities.safety: Move gently. Clear the floor of things to trip on.

schedule.what: Act out the stages of life with your body, from baby to elder and back.

activities.record: Draw yourself in your favourite pose from the parade, and label the life stage.
activities.context: This is a movement activity. You act out each life stage with your body, from a curled-up baby to an elder, to feel how bodies change.

setup.art: A child curled up small on a mat like a newborn baby.
setup.caption: 1. Start curled up, like a newborn.

setup.art: The same child crawling, then toddling with arms out for balance.
setup.caption: 2. Crawl, then take wobbly first steps.

setup.art: The child standing tall and stretched, then walking slowly with a pretend walking stick and a smile.
setup.caption: 3. Grow tall, then walk slowly like an elder.

flow.do: Call out each stage slowly, and move together: newborn, crawling baby, toddler, child running, teenager growing tall, strong adult, elder walking carefully.
flow.say: Curl up small like a newborn. Now crawl. Now take your first wobbly steps. Now run and jump like a child. Now stretch up tall, a teenager growing fast. Now carry heavy shopping like an adult. Now walk slowly and carefully, like an elder on a wet floor.
flow.kid: Curl up like a baby. Crawl. Wobble like a toddler. Run like a child. Stretch tall. Walk slowly like an elder.
flow.parent: When acting as elders, keep it respectful. Elders walk carefully because a fall can break thinner bones, not because they are silly.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Life Stage Parade. You act out each stage of life with your body.

flow.do: Stop and talk.
flow.say: When you were an elder, you walked slowly and carefully. Why do you think elders do that?
flow.kid: Why do elders walk carefully? What could happen if they fell?

check.q: In the parade, you walked carefully like an elder. Why do many elders walk carefully on wet floors?
options: Their bones are thinner, so a fall can break one more easily
check.why: Bones slowly lose some of their hard minerals with age, so a fall can break them more easily. Picking 'always tired' is a guess about elders that is often not true. Many elders are very active.

flow.think: What could you change at home to make floors safer for an elder?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Life Stage Parade. You talk about why elders move the way they do.

activities.title: In Their Shoes: Gloves and Buttons

materials.item: a pair of thick socks or woollen gloves to wear on the hands
a shirt with buttons
5 coins on a table
an old pair of sunglasses with a little petroleum jelly smeared on them, or a piece of butter paper to look through

activities.safety: Never walk around while wearing the smeared glasses. Sit down for every task.

schedule.what: Try everyday tasks with socks on your hands and smeared glasses. Then think about how to help.

activities.record: Write which task was hardest, and one idea to make it easier for an elder.
activities.context: This is an empathy activity. You wear thick socks on your hands and smeared glasses to feel a little of what stiff fingers and older eyes can be like, then think of ways to help.

setup.art: A child sitting at a table wearing thick socks on both hands, trying to pick up a coin.
setup.caption: 1. Put thick socks on your hands. Try to pick up coins.

setup.art: The same child in gloves struggling to do up a shirt button.
setup.caption: 2. Try to do up a button.

setup.art: The child sitting still, looking through blurry smeared glasses at a printed page.
setup.caption: 3. Sit down, and look at small print through smeared glasses.

flow.do: 1. Time how long it takes to pick up 5 coins with bare hands, then with socks on your hands. 2. Try to do up 3 buttons with the socks on. 3. Sitting down, try to read small print through the smeared glasses.
flow.say: As people get older, fingers can get stiff, and touch can feel less sharp. Eyes can get blurry for close things. This is a small taste of that. It is not a game to laugh at elders. It is a way to understand them.
flow.kid: Pick up coins with bare hands. Then with socks on your hands. Try buttons with socks on. Sit down and look through the smeared glasses.
flow.context: This is the first step of In Their Shoes. You try tasks in thick gloves and smeared glasses.

flow.do: Think together about ways to help.
flow.say: What was hardest? Now let's be inventors. How could we make that task easier for an elder?
flow.kid: Which task was hardest? Think of a way to make it easier for an elder.

ask.q: How could we make buttons easier for stiff fingers?
good: Help them, but only if they want help.

check.q: In this activity, you wore thick socks on your hands. Which change in older bodies were the socks a model of?
options: Stiffer joints and less sharp touch in the fingers
check.why: The socks made your fingers clumsy and less able to feel, a bit like stiff joints and duller touch in some elders' hands. They are not a model of height or hearing. The smeared glasses were the model of older eyes.

flow.parent: Gently point out that many elders are proud and capable. Good help means asking first, 'Would you like help?'
flow.context: This is the last step of In Their Shoes. You think of ways to help elders.

activities.title: The Sticky-Note Body

materials.item: a big sheet of paper or newspaper with a body outline drawn on it
about 40 sticky notes or paper squares, in two colours
a pencil

schedule.what: Model how the body replaces some cells fast, some slowly and some never.

activities.record: Draw your body outline and colour the parts that are replaced fast, slowly and never.
activities.context: This is a model activity. Sticky notes stand for cells in a paper body. You replace some notes quickly, some slowly and some never, to see how a body changes while staying the same body.

setup.art: A big paper body outline on the floor covered with yellow sticky notes, labelled skin, blood, bones, brain and eye.
setup.caption: 1. Cover a paper body with yellow notes. Each note is a group of cells.

setup.art: A child peeling yellow notes off the skin and blood areas and sticking on pink ones.
setup.caption: 2. Each 'month', swap the skin and blood notes for new ones.

setup.art: The body outline with most notes pink, but the brain and eye notes still yellow.
setup.caption: 3. After many 'years', look at what is new and what is still old.

flow.do: 1. Draw a big body outline. 2. Cover it with yellow sticky notes. 3. Label areas: skin, blood, gut, bones, brain, eye lens.
flow.say: Each yellow note is a group of cells. This is you, on the day you were born.
flow.kid: Cover the body with yellow notes. Each note is a group of cells. This is you as a newborn.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Sticky-Note Body. You make a paper body covered with paper 'cells'.

flow.do: Call out time passing. Each time, swap notes for pink ones. Every 'week': swap gut notes. Every 'month': swap skin notes. Every '4 months': swap blood notes. Every '10 years': swap bone notes. Never swap brain or eye lens notes.
flow.say: One week passes. Swap the gut. One month passes. Swap the skin. Four months pass. Swap the blood. Ten years pass. Swap the bones. What about the brain and the eye lens? We leave them.
flow.kid: Time passes! Swap the gut notes every week. Skin every month. Blood every 4 months. Bones every 10 years. Leave brain and eye.
flow.parent: These are rough times. Real cells are replaced a few at a time, all the time, not all at once.
flow.context: This is the main step of the Sticky-Note Body. You swap paper 'cells' at different speeds.

flow.do: Look at the body together.
flow.say: Most of this body is new now. Some parts are as old as you. Is it still the same person?
flow.kid: Most notes are new now. Some are still old. Is it still you?

check.q: In the sticky-note model, which notes were never swapped, because those cells stay with you all your life?
options: The brain and eye lens notes
check.why: Most cells in the thinking part of your brain, and the cells in the middle of your eye lens, stay with you all your life. Skin is replaced about every month and red blood cells about every four months.

flow.think: If your body is always changing, what is the 'you' that stays?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Sticky-Note Body. You look at what is new and what is old.

activities.title: My Life Line

materials.item: photos of your child at different ages, and of an elder at different ages if you have them, or drawings
a long strip of paper, about 1 metre, or a string and clothes pegs
a pencil and glue

activities.safety: Ask before using family photos. Use copies, not precious originals.

schedule.what: Make a life line of photos or drawings from birth to now, and from birth to old age for an elder.

activities.record: Your finished life line, with each life stage labelled.
activities.context: In this activity you make a life line: a long strip of paper with photos or drawings of a person at different ages, from baby to now.

setup.art: A long paper strip on the floor marked with years 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, with baby photos and drawings stuck along it.
setup.caption: 1. Mark years along a long paper strip.

setup.art: A child sticking a photo of a toddler at the 2-year mark.
setup.caption: 2. Stick photos or drawings at the right ages.

setup.art: A second, much longer strip above the first, with a grandmother's photos from girl to elder.
setup.caption: 3. Make a second, longer line for an elder.

flow.do: 1. Mark 0, 1, 2 and so on up to your child's age on the strip. 2. Stick a photo or drawing at each age. 3. Under each, write one change: first tooth, first steps, lost a milk tooth.
flow.say: This is your life so far. Let's put a picture at each age and write what changed.
flow.kid: Mark your ages on the strip. Stick a photo or drawing at each. Write what changed.
flow.context: This is the first step of My Life Line. You make a line of your own life so far.

flow.do: Make a longer line for an elder, with their help, from girl or boy to now. Label the stages.

challenges.title: Design an Elder-Friendly Room
challenges.problem: An elder is coming to stay. Small things look blurry to them, their knees are stiff, they hear quiet sounds less well, and their bones break easily in a fall. Design a room that keeps them safe and happy.
constraints: Use a shoebox, cardboard and paper to make a model, or draw a plan.
You must solve at least four problems: seeing, hearing, walking and getting up.
The room must still feel like a home, not a hospital.
materials: small things like buttons, matchboxes and straws for furniture
general: Put a rubber mat on the bathroom floor so it is less slippery.
Fix a handrail next to the bed and the toilet.
Add a small night light so the way to the bathroom is never dark.
Write labels and phone numbers in big, dark letters.
creative: A doorbell that flashes a light as well as ringing, for ears that hear less.
A chair a little higher than usual, so it is easier to stand up from.
A shelf at waist height so nobody has to bend or climb.
A big-button phone with photos of family on the buttons instead of numbers.
challenges.your_turn: Now ask a real elder what would help them most. Change your design, and see if they like it.

challenges.title: The Easy-Open Jar
challenges.problem: Many elders find tight jar lids hard to open, because their hands grip less strongly. Invent a way to open a tight jar with less grip.
constraints: You cannot use a knife or anything sharp.
Use only things found at home.
Test each idea by opening the same jar.
materials: a jar with a screw lid, closed tightly by a grown-up
rubber bands, a rubber glove, a cloth, a wooden spoon, a belt or strap
general: Put a wide rubber band around the lid. It gives the hand more grip.
Hold the lid with a rubber glove or a dry cloth.
Tap the edge of the lid gently on the table to loosen it.
creative: Wrap a belt around the lid and pull the end. The longer handle turns the lid with less force, like a lever.
Put a wooden spoon handle through a rubber band around the lid, and turn the spoon like a spanner.
Hold a metal lid under warm tap water for a minute. Metal grows very slightly bigger when warm, so the lid loosens.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own jar opener. Draw it, make it and test it. Give the best one to an elder you know.
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You invent ways to open a tight jar lid with less grip, to help elders whose hands have got weaker with age.

quiz.p: Which list shows the life stages in the right order?
opts: Baby, child, teenager, adult, older adult
Child, baby, adult, teenager, older adult
Baby, teenager, child, older adult, adult
Adult, child, baby, teenager, older adult
quiz.why: Every person goes through the stages in this order. Picking a mixed-up order often means teenager and child have been confused.

quiz.p: A baby grows from about 50 cm to about 75 cm in a year. What does this tell us?
opts: Babies grow faster than at any other age
Babies stop growing after one year
quiz.why: The first year is the fastest growth of a whole life. Children grow only about 5 to 6 cm a year. Picking 'everyone' means growth has been pictured as steady.

quiz.p: Why does a grandfather hold his newspaper far away to read it?
opts: The lens in his eye has got stiffer and cannot focus up close
quiz.why: A stiffer lens cannot bulge to focus on close things. Picking 'arms got longer' turns his joke into a fact. Eyes do not shrink with age.

quiz.p: Why does an elder's hair look grey from far away?
opts: It is a mix of white hairs with no colour and some dark hairs
quiz.why: Pigment cells at the roots run out, so new hairs grow white. Mixed with dark ones, they look grey. Already-grown hair cannot change colour overnight.

quiz.p: Meera, a girl in Class 3, gently pinched the skin on the back of her own hand. It went flat in less than 1 second. Her grandmother's skin took 3 seconds. Why?
opts: Older skin has fewer springy threads inside
Children's skin has no threads in it
quiz.why: Collagen and elastin threads make skin springy, and older skin has fewer. In a fair test, everyone is pinched the same way, so the pinch was not the cause.

chart.title: Made-up results: seconds for pinched skin to go flat

quiz.p: In the skin test, you pinch the back of a hand and count how long the skin takes to go flat. To make it fair, what must stay the same for everyone?
opts: The place pinched and how long it is pinched
quiz.why: In a fair test you change only the thing you are testing, here the age. Everything else, like the place and time of the pinch, stays the same.

quiz.p: Which of these is true about the cells in your body?
opts: Many are replaced all the time, but some stay all your life
They are all as old as you
quiz.why: Skin, blood and gut cells are replaced often. Most brain cells and eye lens cells stay all life. Picking '7 years' repeats a popular saying that is not true.

quiz.p: Which of these can keep getting better as people grow old?
quiz.why: Knowledge and words can grow all life long. Hearing high sounds and reading tiny print usually get harder. Growing taller stops in the late teens.

quiz.p: What is the best way to help an elder who finds a task hard?
opts: Ask if they would like help, then help in the way they want
Do everything for them without asking
Tell them they are too old
quiz.why: Elders are capable people. Good help starts by asking. Doing everything without asking can make someone feel they are not trusted.

quiz.p: Can a person of 90 make their muscles stronger?
opts: Yes, muscles respond to exercise at any age
No, it is too late after 60
Only if they were athletes when young
quiz.why: In 1990, people aged about 90 got much stronger in eight weeks of strength exercise. Picking 'too late' is a common belief that the evidence disproves.

quiz.p: What do scientists agree on about ageing?
opts: Exercise, good food, sleep and friends help at every age
That ageing will be cured soon
quiz.why: Many large studies show healthy habits help at every age. Why bodies age, and whether it can be cured, are still argued about.

quiz.p: Why did life expectancy in India rise from about 32 years in 1951 to about 70 today?
opts: Clean water, vaccines, better food and doctors saved many babies and children
Bodies became made of different cells
quiz.why: Most of the change came from far fewer babies and children dying of illnesses. Picking 'more birthdays' mixes up counting years with the reasons people live longer.

quiz.p: What happens at the end of every life cycle?
opts: The living thing dies, and its atoms return to the soil, water and air
It starts again as a baby the next day
It turns into a different animal
quiz.why: Death is the last stage of every life cycle, for plants, animals and people. The atoms of the body are not lost but become part of other living things. Families have many different beliefs about what happens after death.

quiz.p: Telomeres are tiny caps on the ends of the threads that hold our genes. What happens to them in many cells?
opts: They get shorter each time the cell splits
quiz.why: In many cells the caps shorten with each split. When they get too short, the cell stops splitting. Elizabeth Blackburn and Carol Greider found the substance that can rebuild them.

opts: Grandmothers who helped care for grandchildren helped humans evolve long lives
quiz.why: Kristen Hawkes and her team suggested this in 1998. Killer whale grandmothers that lead their families to food fit the idea. Other scientists think there are other reasons too, so it is debated.

applications: Doctors and health workers check babies' height and weight on growth charts to see they are growing well.
Eye doctors test the near point and prescribe reading glasses for people over 40.
Hearing tests use high and low beeps, just like the high sound test, to find hearing loss early.
Builders add ramps, handrails and non-slip tiles to homes, stations and temples so elders can move safely.
Phones and tablets have big-text and loud settings for older eyes and ears.
Bus and train seats are kept for senior citizens, because standing in a moving vehicle can cause falls.
Doctors called geriatricians specialise in caring for elders.
Physiotherapists teach elders strength and balance exercises to prevent falls.
Scientists study tiny worms, flies and hydras to learn how ageing works.
Vaccines given to babies are one big reason people now live longer.
Sunscreen, hats and shade slow down skin wrinkling caused by strong sun.
Pension schemes and senior citizen discounts help elders who no longer earn a salary.
Day care centres for elders give company, games and exercise, which help body and mind.

open_questions.q: Why do bodies age at all?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have several ideas: damage building up, shortening caps on genes, and nature's timetable. They do not agree which matters most.

open_questions.q: Is there a limit to how long a human can live?
open_questions.why_open: The oldest checked person lived to 122. Some scientists think about 120 is a natural limit. Others think there is no fixed limit.

open_questions.q: How do some animals, like hydras, seem not to age?
open_questions.why_open: Hydras keep making new cells for their whole bodies. Scientists are still finding out how, and whether they truly never age.

open_questions.q: How many new brain cells does an older brain make?
open_questions.why_open: Some studies find many new brain cells in elders, and others find almost none. Scientists are still checking how to count them properly.

open_questions.q: Can ageing be slowed in humans?
open_questions.why_open: It has been slowed in worms, flies and mice. Nobody has shown it safely in people yet.

open_questions.q: Why do some people go grey at 30 and others at 70?
open_questions.why_open: Genes play a big part, and stress may too. Scientists are still finding out exactly how.

open_questions.q: If almost all your cells change, what makes you the same person?
open_questions.why_open: This is a question for science and philosophy. Some say memory, some say the pattern of your body, and some say awareness itself. Nobody has a final answer.

maths.problem: In the near point test, a child read tiny print at 10 cm. A grandmother needed it 60 cm away. How many times further away did the grandmother need it?
maths.explain: The grandmother needed 60 cm. The child needed 10 cm. 60 divided by 10 is 6. You can check: 10 + 10 + 10 + 10 + 10 + 10 = 60.
maths.context: This is about the near point test. You brought a card with tiny print closer to each person's face until it blurred, and measured the distance.

chart.title: Closest distance at which tiny print looked sharp

maths.why_maths: Saying '6 times further' tells us how much the eye has changed, not just that it changed.

maths.problem: Riya, a girl in Class 3, did the skin test with her Dadi, her father's mother. Dadi's three tries took 4 seconds, 2 seconds and 3 seconds. What is the middle value?
maths.explain: Put the numbers in order, smallest first: 2, 3, 4. The number in the middle is 3. So the middle value is 3 seconds.
maths.context: This is about the snap-back skin test. You gently pinched the back of a hand for 3 seconds and counted how long the skin took to go flat. You did it 3 times for each person.
maths.why_maths: One try can be a fluke. The middle value gives a fair number that one odd try does not change.

maths.problem: A newborn is about 50 cm long. By its first birthday it is about 75 cm. Later, a child grows about 5 cm a year. How many years does a child take to grow as much as a baby grows in its first year?
maths.explain: The baby grew 75 minus 50, which is 25 cm, in one year. A child grows 5 cm a year. 25 divided by 5 is 5. So a child takes 5 years to grow what a baby grows in one.
maths.context: This is about the life line you made, with photos of yourself at each age. Babies grow much faster than older children.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two speeds shows how much faster babies grow than children.

maths.problem: In 1951, life expectancy in India was about 32 years. Today it is about 70 years. How many more years can a baby born today expect to live?
maths.explain: 70 minus 32. First 70 minus 30 is 40. Then 40 minus 2 is 38. So about 38 more years.
maths.context: This is about the card on people living longer than ever before. Clean water, vaccines and doctors have helped babies and children survive.
maths.show: Two bars: India 1951 and India today.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting shows exactly how many years of life clean water, vaccines and doctors have added.

maths.problem: In your interview, the elder is 68 years old and you are 8. How many years ago was the elder your age? If this year is 2026, what year was that?
maths.explain: 68 minus 8 is 60. So the elder was 8 years old 60 years ago. 2026 minus 60 is 1966.
maths.context: This is about the Interview an Elder activity, where you asked an elder about their life when they were your age.
maths.why_maths: Working out the year helps you picture the world the elder grew up in.

maths.problem: A red blood cell lasts about 4 months. A year has 12 months. About how many times are your red blood cells replaced in one year?
maths.explain: 12 divided by 4 is 3. So your red blood cells are replaced about 3 times a year. You can check: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
maths.context: This is about the Sticky-Note Body, where you swapped paper 'cells' at different speeds. Blood notes were swapped every 4 months.
maths.why_maths: Dividing shows how fast the body renews itself, even though we do not notice it.

roots.context: We have been learning how a body changes over a whole life, from baby to elder. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Your skin and blood are replaced again and again, but your eye lens never throws a cell away. It keeps adding new layers around the old ones, so it grows thicker and stiffer every year. That is why the near point test found older people holding print further away. So some ageing comes from what a body keeps, like the old cells in the lens.
deep_truth.habit: We think of ageing as a body wearing out, like an old chappal. The lens shows another way: it gets older because it keeps every cell it has ever made.
deep_truth.evidence: In the near point test, a child reads tiny print at about 8 centimetres, while many people over 45 need 30 centimetres or more. The cells in the middle of the lens were made before birth, and the lens keeps growing all life.

three.who_am_i: Your size, skin and hair all change over your life. Some parts of you, like the middle of your eye lens, have been with you since before you were born.
three.what_is_life: A living body is always making new cells and clearing away old ones, from birth to the end of its life.
three.what_is_this_world: Seeds, trees, rivers and people all change through stages. Nothing in the world stays exactly the same.

roots.thread: A body is always being taken apart and built again. Food brings in new atoms, and old cells are broken down and carried away. Skin, blood and gut are renewed again and again, while the eye lens and most brain cells stay. When a body dies, its atoms return to the soil and air and become part of plants and other living things. So the atoms in a grandmother and in her grandchild came from the same soil, water and air, and will go back to them.

teachings.teaching: The one who lives in this body passes through childhood, youth and old age. The wise are not confused by these changes.
teachings.link: The body changes at every stage, but the Gita says something in us stays the same through all of them. Science shows the body really does change, cell by cell.

teachings.source: Heraclitus, the Greek thinker, as quoted in Plato's Cratylus 402a
teachings.teaching: You cannot step into the same river twice. The water is always new, yet we still call it the same river.
teachings.link: Your body is like the river. Its cells are always being replaced, but we still call it you.

teachings.teaching: There is a time for everything. A time to be born and a time to die. A time to plant and a time to harvest.
teachings.link: Every life has its stages, in order, and each stage has its own work: babies learn to walk, elders teach and remember.

science.text: Your body makes millions of new cells every second, mostly blood cells. Yet most brain cells and the cells at the centre of your eye lens stay with you all your life.
When a body dies, its atoms are not lost. They return to the soil, water and air, and become part of other living things.

other_view.who: The Buddha, and many neuroscientists today
other_view.view: The Buddha taught anatta, that there is no fixed self going through the stages. There is only the changing itself, moment to moment. Many neuroscientists also think 'you' is a pattern your brain makes, which changes as the brain changes. Both are honest views worth thinking about.

practice.title: Hands across time
practice.say: Let's put our hands flat on the table, side by side. Look at your hand. Now look at mine. Close your eyes and breathe in slowly. Picture your hand as a tiny baby's hand, curled up. Breathe out. Now picture it as an old person's hand, with soft lines and spots. Breathe in. It is the same hand. Open your eyes. Your hand will change for the rest of your life. Will the one looking at it change too?
practice.kid: Put your hand flat on the table. Look at it. Close your eyes and breathe slowly. Picture it as a baby's hand. Now picture it very old and wrinkled. It is the same hand. Will the one looking at it change too?

ask: If all your cells change, what is it that stays 'you'?
Is the baby in your old photo you, or someone else?
What do you think you will know when you are 80, that you do not know now?
When an old tree falls and becomes soil for new trees, has it ended, or changed?

how_we_found_out.story: In 1912, the French surgeon Alexis Carrel began growing cells from a chicken embryo's heart in a glass dish. He fed them a juice made from crushed chicken embryos. He said the cells kept splitting and growing for more than 30 years, longer than a chicken lives. So most scientists came to believe that cells, kept in a dish, could live for ever. Ageing, they thought, came from the body around the cells, not from the cells. In 1961, Leonard Hayflick and Paul Moorhead in Philadelphia grew human cells. Their cells always slowed and stopped after about 40 to 60 splits. Many scientists thought they had made a mistake. So they mixed old cells from a man with young cells from a woman, in the same dish. The old male cells stopped first, while the young female cells kept splitting. So the dish was not to blame. The cells were counting their own splits. Many scientists now think fresh living cells came into Carrel's dishes with the embryo juice.
how_we_found_out.who: Alexis Carrel, a French surgeon, and Leonard Hayflick and Paul Moorhead, two American scientists
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Cells kept in a dish can split for ever, so ageing comes only from the body around them. Hayflick and Moorhead showed that human cells stop after about 40 to 60 splits, even in a dish.
